lines.trans: Chef, those were just coconuts.
Be quiet right now, Fedya!
I will bring him to his senses now.
Stand right there!
Chef, excuse me, please.
Please do not kill me.
We do not wish you any harm.
Then why did you hit me?
This is just a foolish misunderstanding.
Let me go from here, please.
Of course, you are completely free.
Do you want to go to your room?
Fedya, escort the man, please.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, it (is)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: It overshadowed that unpleasant incident.
What kind of total nonsense is this?
Chef, those were just coconuts.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Yes, it is just so unexpected.
Your signature set is simply excellent.
Chef, those were just coconuts.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'coconuts' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: People die from falling coconuts.
A coconut has already fallen on me.
You will not withstand a blow from a coconut.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'молчать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'shut up, be quiet', paired with 'молчать'.

examples.trans: Lieutenant Sokolov, be quiet!
Everyone fell silent at once.
Shut up and stop frightening us.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: You must not be overfed right now.
Maybe tomorrow, or maybe right now.
Let us test it right now!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'but, after all', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: A coconut has already fallen on me.
Well, I am completely alive.
Let us make a bet then.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'вести'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to bring, to lead (someone somewhere)', paired with 'приводить'.

examples.trans: Bring him tomorrow to the hospital.
The father brought his son to the doctor.
You will bring the child in the morning.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'his', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: It overshadowed that unpleasant incident.
Of course, you are completely free.
What kind of report will he write now?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello, Viktor Petrovich.
I am inspecting your restaurant.
Is everything alright with you?

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'feeling, emotion, sense' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I will bring him to his senses now.

examples.text: Шеф, я приведу вас в чувство!
examples.trans: Chef, I will bring you to your senses!

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович испытывает к вам чувства.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich has feelings for you.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'тоять'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'stop, wait', paired with 'постоять'.

examples.trans: The hotel guests are complaining about loud noise.
We are true keepers of secrets.
I constantly cleaned up after you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Do not look at me like that.
A coconut has already fallen on me.
I hope everything will be great for us.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'place' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Stand right there!
We want to compensate your damage.
This is my seat.

meanings.note: Prefix 'из-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (stem 'винить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'excuse me', paired with 'извинять'.

examples.trans: Chef, excuse me, please.
Sorry, Chef, I gave you away.
Sorry, I'm in a hurry.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'me', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Do not look at me like that.
You must not be overfed right now.
I am inspecting your restaurant.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'жалуйста').

examples.trans: Chef, excuse me, please.
Please do not kill me.
Let me go from here, please.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Do not look at me like that.
You must not be overfed right now.
Yes, it is just so unexpected.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'бивать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'kill', paired with 'убить'.

examples.trans: Please do not kill me.
Please, help! They're killing me!
Don't waste time for nothing.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We will wash everything out quickly.
We will fix everything!
We do not wish you any harm.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to wish', paired with 'пожелать'.

examples.trans: We do not wish you any harm.
Good health to you, sir! (I wish you health!)
I wish you happiness.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Just do not worry.
You will not withstand a blow from a coconut.
I will not withstand such a blow?

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'evil; harm' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Evil always comes back.
I don't mean any harm.

examples.text: Запомните: зло всегда возвращается к правителю.
examples.trans: Remember: evil always comes back to the ruler.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Do not look at me like that.
You must not be overfed right now.
Hello, Viktor Petrovich.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'why', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Then why did you hit me?

meanings.en: to hit, to strike, to punch
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'дарить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to hit, to strike', paired with 'ударять'.

examples.trans: Then why did you hit me?
Lightning just struck me.
Well, come on, hit me!

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('silly, foolish').

examples.trans: This is just a foolish misunderstanding.
How foolish you are!
Vanya, are you stupid?

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'доразумение'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'misunderstanding' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is just a foolish misunderstanding.
There was a terrible misunderstanding this morning.
It's just a misunderstanding.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'пустить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'let go, release', paired with 'отпускать'.

examples.trans: Let me go from here, please.
If we let him go, he will create problems.
Viktor Petrovich, please let us go.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'сюда').

examples.trans: Let me go from here, please.
That is it, go away from here quickly.
Hand it here and get out of here.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Of course, you are completely free.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'овершенно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Of course, you are completely free.

examples.text: Совершенно верно, я мэр этого города.
examples.trans: Quite right, I am the mayor of this town.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'вободный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('free').

examples.trans: Of course, you are completely free.
That's all, you can go!
Is this seat free?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: He wanted to speak with the chef.

examples.trans: Fedya, escort the man, please.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'person' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Fedya, escort the man, please.

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'ъяснить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'will explain', paired with 'объяснять'.
